title: How does AQE handle data skew — it detects skewed shuffle partitions (via `skewedPartitionFactor` and `skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes`), splits them into smaller pieces, and replicates the other side — and when might you still need manual salting?
shortTitle: How AQE handles data skew (and when you still need salting)

s1_definition.profdef: AQE handles data skew in joins by detecting shuffle partitions that are abnormally large — specifically those whose size exceeds both the skewed-partition factor times the median partition size and the skewed-partition threshold in bytes — and splitting each such partition into several smaller sub-partitions. It then replicates the matching rows from the other side of the join so each sub-partition can be joined independently, which spreads a hot key's work across many tasks. Manual salting is still needed when a single key's data is so large that even one sub-partition is unbalanced, or when the skewed operation is not a join that AQE's skew handling covers.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine combining two lists at the National Bank of India, and almost all the activity belongs to one giant corporate account. After the re-sort, one clerk is buried under a mountain of that account's slips while everyone else has a light load, so that one clerk finishes hours after the rest and the whole report waits on them. AQE is the supervisor who spots the mountain, splits it into several smaller piles handed to several clerks, and gives each of those clerks a copy of the matching records they need, so the mountain is cleared in parallel. But if that one account is so colossal that even the split piles are still huge, the supervisor must do something cleverer up front — tagging each slip with a random sub-label so the account spreads evenly from the start. That up-front tagging is salting.
s1_definition.oneliner: AQE kills join stragglers by detecting skewed partitions through a factor-of-median and byte threshold, splitting them, and replicating the other side; salting is the manual fallback for extreme or non-join skew.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** AQE handles data skew in joins by detecting shuffle partitions that are abnormally large — specifically those whose size exceeds both the skewed-partition factor times the median partition size and the skewed-partition threshold in bytes — and splitting each such partition into several smaller sub-partitions. It then replicates the matching rows from the other side of the join so each sub-partition can be joined independently, which spreads a hot key's work across many tasks. Manual salting is still needed when a single key's data is so large that even one sub-partition is unbalanced, or when the skewed operation is not a join that AQE's skew handling covers.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine combining two lists at the National Bank of India, and almost all the activity belongs to one giant corporate account. After the re-sort, one clerk is buried under a mountain of that account's slips while everyone else has a light load, so that one clerk finishes hours after the rest and the whole report waits on them. AQE is the supervisor who spots the mountain, splits it into several smaller piles handed to several clerks, and gives each of those clerks a copy of the matching records they need, so the mountain is cleared in parallel. But if that one account is so colossal that even the split piles are still huge, the supervisor must do something cleverer up front — tagging each slip with a random sub-label so the account spreads evenly from the start. That up-front tagging is salting.

**One line to remember:** AQE kills join stragglers by detecting skewed partitions through a factor-of-median and byte threshold, splitting them, and replicating the other side; salting is the manual fallback for extreme or non-join skew.

sections.s2_technical:
Data skew is when the values of a join or grouping key are distributed very unevenly, so one key, or a few keys, carry far more rows than the rest. After the shuffle that a join requires, all rows for a key land in one partition, so a hot key produces one giant partition while the others are small. Spark runs one task per partition, so the task on that giant partition runs long after all the others complete — a straggler — and the whole stage is only as fast as its slowest task. Worse, that task can exhaust executor memory and fail.

AQE detects this at the shuffle boundary using two thresholds that must both be met. The skewed-partition factor, defaulting to five, requires the partition to be larger than that many times the median partition size, which catches partitions that are outliers relative to the rest. The skewed-partition threshold in bytes, defaulting to two hundred fifty-six megabytes, requires the partition to be large in absolute terms, which avoids treating a small-but-relatively-large partition as skewed on a tiny dataset. Requiring both conditions prevents false positives.

Once a partition is flagged as skewed, AQE splits it into several smaller sub-partitions along the skewed side. Crucially, to still produce correct join results, it replicates the matching rows from the other side of the join into each sub-partition, so every sub-partition has both its slice of the skewed side and the full set of matching rows it needs. Each sub-partition is then joined independently as its own task, so the hot key's work is parallelized across many tasks instead of crushing one. This is why it is specifically called skew join optimization — it is tailored to the join case and needs the replicate-other-side step to stay correct.

A senior nuance is knowing when AQE is not enough and manual salting is required. First, if a single key is so dominant that even one sub-partition is still too large, splitting cannot help because all those rows share the same key and must still be processed together on the skewed side; salting addresses this by appending a random suffix to the key so that one logical key becomes many physical keys that distribute evenly, with a matching expansion on the other side. Second, AQE's skew handling targets joins, so heavily skewed aggregations or window operations may still need salting or a pre-aggregation step. Third, salting is also the tool when you must control skew before a shuffle rather than react to it after. In the bank, AQE handled the everyday moderate skew of busy branches automatically, but for a handful of mega-corporate accounts whose volume dwarfed everything else, we still salted the join key so those accounts spread evenly from the start.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — One corporate account's transactions create a giant partition and a straggler task. This is exactly the skew AQE detects and splits.

Problem 2 — Splitting must keep join results correct. This is exactly why AQE replicates the other side into each sub-partition.

Problem 3 — One account is so dominant that even splits are unbalanced. This is exactly when manual salting is required.

The mini-project models skew in Java. A `SkewDetector` flags partitions that exceed both the factor-of-median and byte threshold. A `SkewSplitter` splits a flagged partition and replicates the dimension side. A `Salter` demonstrates the manual fallback by adding random suffixes to a mega-key. The demo joins Rajesh's and Priya's accounts against a hugely skewed corporate account and shows detection, splitting, and salting.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three join-key partitions — Rajesh at twenty megabytes, Priya at eighteen megabytes, and a corporate mega-account at one gigabyte. The skew factor is five, and the byte threshold is two hundred fifty-six megabytes.

Step 1: The detector computes the median partition size, which is around twenty megabytes. It then checks each partition against both conditions.

Step 2: Rajesh and Priya are near the median, so they fail the relative test and are left alone. The corporate account at one gigabyte is more than five times the median and more than two hundred fifty-six megabytes, so it passes both tests and is flagged as skewed.

Step 3: The splitter divides the one-gigabyte partition into several sub-partitions sized near the target, so the corporate account's work is spread across multiple tasks instead of one straggler.

Step 4: To keep the join correct, the matching dimension rows for the corporate account are replicated into each sub-partition, so every sub-task has both its slice of the skewed side and the full matching rows it needs.

Step 5: In this extreme case the single corporate key is so dominant that even the sub-partitions remain large, because all those rows share one key, so AQE's split alone is not enough and manual salting is applied.

Step 6: Salting appends a random suffix to the corporate key on the fact side so it spreads across eight buckets, and expands the single dimension row into eight salted copies so the join still matches. The journey shows AQE handling ordinary skew automatically and salting as the deliberate fallback for an extreme single key.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [WARNING] SKEW detected: key 'CORP9999' 1000000000B (median=20000000, >5x AND >threshold)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] split 'CORP9999' into 4 sub-partitions; replicate 1 dimension rows into each (join stays correct)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] CORP9999 still dominates even after split → apply manual salting
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] salted fact key 'CORP9999' across 8 buckets
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] expanded dimension key 'CORP9999' into 8 salted copies (so the join still matches)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Join-key partitions: SAV2001(20MB) CUR3001(18MB) CORP9999(1000MB)
    │
    ▼  AQE SkewDetector: > 5×median(20MB) AND > 256MB ?
  SAV2001 no    CUR3001 no    CORP9999 YES ──→ skewed
    │
    ▼  AQE SkewSplitter
  CORP9999 → [#sub0 250MB][#sub1 250MB][#sub2 250MB][#sub3 250MB]
             + replicate dimension rows into EACH sub (join correct)
    │
    ▼  Still one dominant key? → MANUAL SALTING
  fact:  CORP9999 → CORP9999_0 .. CORP9999_7   (random suffix)
  dim :  CORP9999 → copy to _0 .. _7            (expand to match)
    │
    ▼
  Mega key now spreads evenly across 8 buckets from the start
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
AQE handles data skew in joins, which is one of the most common causes of mysterious straggler tasks. Skew happens when a join key is distributed very unevenly, so after the shuffle that a join requires, all the rows for a hot key land in one partition, producing one giant partition among many small ones. Since Spark runs one task per partition, the task on that giant partition runs long after all the others finish and can even run out of memory, and the whole stage is only as fast as that slowest task.

AQE detects this at the shuffle boundary using two conditions that must both be satisfied: the skewed-partition factor, defaulting to five, requires the partition to be larger than five times the median partition size, and the skewed-partition threshold in bytes, defaulting to two hundred fifty-six megabytes, requires it to be large in absolute terms. Requiring both avoids false positives on tiny datasets. Once a partition is flagged, AQE splits it into several smaller sub-partitions along the skewed side, and critically it replicates the matching rows from the other side of the join into each sub-partition so the results stay correct, after which each sub-partition is joined as its own task and the hot key's work is parallelized instead of crushing one task.

In my project at the National Bank of India, AQE's skew handling automatically smoothed out the everyday moderate skew of busy branches, which was a big reliability win because those used to cause random slow stages. But I always explain when AQE is not enough and manual salting is needed. If a single key is so dominant that even one sub-partition is still too large, splitting cannot help because all those rows share the same key, so I salt the key by appending a random suffix on the fact side and expanding the matching row into one copy per salt bucket on the dimension side, which spreads that one logical key across many physical keys from the start. Salting is also the tool for heavily skewed aggregations and window operations, which AQE's join-focused skew handling does not cover. For us, a handful of mega-corporate accounts whose volume dwarfed everything else were exactly that case, so we salted their join key while letting AQE handle the rest automatically.
